In /opt/nxeon (production tree — READ-ONLY investigation, do not edit anything), I need a concrete SEO action plan for the Nxeon hosting platform. Three parts:

## Part 1: Diagnose 5 specific striking-distance keyword opportunities

These 5 query+page pairs rank position 23-30 (page 2-3 of Google) with real impressions but ZERO clicks over the last 90 days, per Google Search Console:

1. "vps" (197 impressions, position ~27) → https://nxeon.cloud/blog/what-is-a-vps
2. "palworld vps" (55 impressions, position ~25) → https://nxeon.cloud/blog/best-vps-specs-for-a-palworld-server
3. "vps for business" (22 impressions, position ~24) → https://nxeon.cloud/blog/best-vps-for-a-small-business-website
4. "palworld vps hosting" (18 impressions, position ~27) → same Palworld post as #2
5. "ram needed for game server" (29 impressions, position ~30) → https://nxeon.cloud/blog/how-much-ram-and-cpu-does-a-game-server-need

For EACH one, read the actual page's source file (find it under `app/blog/` — likely `app/blog/[slug]/` with content stored as markdown/DB rows, or check `prisma/seed-blog*.ts`/`scripts/blog-seed-lib.mjs` for where post content actually lives — these may be DB-seeded posts, not static files, so check the database directly if needed via a read-only Prisma query) and diagnose concretely why it's stuck outside page 1 rather than guessing generically. Look for:
- Does the exact query phrase appear in the H1/title/first paragraph? (e.g. does "what is a vps" as a phrase actually appear near the top of that post, or does the post use different wording throughout?)
- Word count / depth — is it thin compared to what typically ranks for a query like "vps" (a highly competitive, high-volume generic term — realistic expectation-setting matters here, "vps" alone is extremely competitive and page-2 for a young site might already be reasonable progress, say so if true rather than promising an easy win)
- Internal linking — does anything else on the site link to this page with relevant anchor text? Check a few other blog posts/pages for links to it.
- Meta title/description — do they match the query intent, or are they generic?
- For the two Palworld posts (#2, #4 point to the same page) — is there a *separate* page specifically for "palworld vps hosting" as a service/landing intent vs this being a blog post (informational intent)? Query intent mismatch (blog content ranking for what might be a more transactional/service-page query) is a common real cause worth checking.
- For "ram needed for game server" → check if the post's title/content actually addresses the general "game server" framing or is narrowly focused on one specific game, which would explain a generic query ranking weakly.

Give a specific, actionable fix per page (e.g. "add an H2 answering '[exact query]' verbatim in the first 100 words", "the post is 400 words on a topic that competitively needs 1200+", "no internal links point here — add 3 links from X, Y, Z pages with anchor text matching the query"). Don't recommend generic SEO advice — ground every recommendation in what you actually found on that specific page.

## Part 2: Are there more pages worth adding?

Read `app/(marketing)/[slug]/page.tsx` (the programmatic city/service matrix) and whatever config drives it (look for a data file listing cities and service types — likely something like `lib/seo-locations.ts` or similar) to see the CURRENT list of cities and service types covered. Also check `app/(marketing)/game-servers/` for which games have dedicated landing pages (cross-reference against `lib/games.ts`'s full GAME_FAMILIES list — are there game families with NO dedicated landing page at all?).

Then, using the GSC data pattern already established (queries mentioning specific games/cities/services that get impressions even at very low volume or beyond position 30 — indicating real search demand Nxeon isn't yet capturing with a dedicated page) as a signal, suggest concrete NEW page opportunities: specific city+service combos not yet covered, specific game families without a landing page, or specific blog topics implied by low-ranking queries that don't have a matching page at all today. Be specific (name the exact city/game/topic), not generic ("add more content").

## Part 3: Does the sitemap need updating?

Find the sitemap generation code (`app/sitemap.xml/route.ts` or similar — there's a route at `/sitemap.xml` per the earlier page inventory). Read it to understand HOW it generates its URL list — is it dynamic (queries the DB/config live, so it auto-includes new blog posts and location-matrix pages as they're added) or does it have a hardcoded/stale list that needs manual maintenance? If dynamic, confirm it would already include today's ~140+ pages including the recent region-tier and city-matrix additions (Aug 29-30 commits) without needing a manual update. If it has ANY hardcoded page lists or appears to be missing recently-added route groups, flag exactly what's missing.

## Output

Report back as three clearly separated sections matching the three parts above. For Part 1, one paragraph of diagnosis + one concrete action per page (5 total). For Part 2, a short list of specific new-page suggestions with the GSC evidence backing each one. For Part 3, a direct yes/no on whether the sitemap needs a manual update, with the specific reason. Keep it concrete and actionable — this will be relayed directly to the site owner to decide what to act on.

A **VPS** — Virtual Private Server — is your own isolated slice of a physical server. One powerful machine is split by a hypervisor into several independent virtual servers, and each one behaves like a dedicated computer: its own operating system, its own users, its own IP address, and a guaranteed share of CPU, RAM and disk.

## How virtualization works

The host machine runs a **hypervisor** (KVM is the industry standard, and what Nxeon uses). The hypervisor carves the hardware into virtual machines. Each VM thinks it owns real hardware — it boots its own Linux kernel, mounts its own disk, and can be rebooted or reinstalled without touching its neighbors.

Crucially, resources are *reserved*, not merely shared. If your plan says 4 GB of RAM, that memory is yours. A busy neighbor cannot eat into it — a problem that plagues cheap shared hosting.

## What "full root access" gives you

On a VPS you get the **root** account, the system administrator. That means you can:

- Install any software: databases, language runtimes, Docker, custom binaries.
- Open and close network ports and configure your own firewall.
- Tune the kernel, mount extra storage, or run background services.
- Reinstall the whole operating system whenever you want.

Shared hosting hides all of this behind a control panel. A VPS hands you the keys.

- **vCPU** — virtual processor cores. More cores means better handling of concurrent work.

- Loading a large base is smooth rather than stuttery.

=== full what-is-a-vps body ===
A **VPS** — Virtual Private Server — is your own isolated slice of a physical server. One powerful machine is split by a hypervisor into several independent virtual servers, and each one behaves like a dedicated computer: its own operating system, its own users, its own IP address, and a guaranteed share of CPU, RAM and disk.

## How virtualization works

The host machine runs a **hypervisor** (KVM is the industry standard, and what Nxeon uses). The hypervisor carves the hardware into virtual machines. Each VM thinks it owns real hardware — it boots its own Linux kernel, mounts its own disk, and can be rebooted or reinstalled without touching its neighbors.

Crucially, resources are *reserved*, not merely shared. If your plan says 4 GB of RAM, that memory is yours. A busy neighbor cannot eat into it — a problem that plagues cheap shared hosting.

## What "full root access" gives you

On a VPS you get the **root** account, the system administrator. That means you can:

- Install any software: databases, language runtimes, Docker, custom binaries.
- Open and close network ports and configure your own firewall.
- Tune the kernel, mount extra storage, or run background services.
- Reinstall the whole operating system whenever you want.

Shared hosting hides all of this behind a control panel. A VPS hands you the keys.

## A quick anatomy

When you order a VPS you'll pick a few things:

- **vCPU** — virtual processor cores. More cores means better handling of concurrent work.
- **RAM** — working memory. This is usually the first thing you run out of.
- **NVMe storage** — fast solid-state disk. NVMe drives are many times faster than the SATA SSDs older hosts still use, which makes databases and file operations snappy.
- **Bandwidth** — how much data you can transfer each month.
- **An operating system image** — Ubuntu, Debian, AlmaLinux, Rocky and so on.

## When is a VPS the right choice?

A VPS is the sweet spot for anyone who has outgrown shared hosting but does not need a whole physical server. Common uses:

- Hosting one or many websites with full control over the stack.
- Running a web app (Node.js, Python, PHP, Go) with its own database.
- Self-hosting tools like Nextcloud, a Git server, or a VPN.
- Development and staging environments.
- Bots, scrapers, cron jobs, and background workers.

## VPS vs the alternatives, in one line each

- **Shared hosting** — cheapest, but you share everything and get no root. Fine for a small brochure site.
- **VPS** — private, root access, guaranteed resources, great price-to-power ratio.
- **Dedicated server** — a whole physical machine; maximum power, maximum cost.
- **Cloud** — a VPS you can spin up, resize and destroy on demand, billed by usage.

## Getting started

With Nxeon, a VPS deploys in about a minute on **NVMe storage** with **full root access** and one-click OS images (Ubuntu, Debian, AlmaLinux, Rocky). You can also pick a **dedicated IP** and, if you'd rather not touch the command line, a one-click control panel like CyberPanel or HestiaCP.

Once it's live, you connect over SSH:

```
ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP
```

From there the server is entirely yours. The rest of this blog walks through securing it, hosting websites and apps, and keeping it fast — but the core idea is simple: a VPS is a real server you fully control, at a fraction of the price of owning the hardware.

Most small-business sites — a brochure site, a WordPress site, a booking page — are light. The priorities are **reliability, speed and a professional setup**, not raw power:

None of this requires you to be a sysadmin — one-click images and managed options handle the heavy lifting.

The quiet advantage of starting on a VPS is that it grows with the business. A brochure site today can become a booking system, an online store, or a customer portal tomorrow — all on the same server, or a quick resize to a bigger plan when traffic climbs. You're never forced to migrate to a different kind of hosting just because you added a feature.

- **Add a database, an app, or a store** whenever you're ready — full root, no artificial limits.

If your site is important to your business, a VPS is worth it. Dedicated resources mean faster, more reliable performance than oversold shared hosting, plus full control over security, email and backups.

Investigation complete. Full findings below.

## Part 1: Striking-distance keyword diagnosis

All five pages are DB-backed `BlogPost` rows (Prisma model at `prisma/schema.prisma:1811`, rendered by `/opt/nxeon/app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx`, content queried live — not static files). I read each post's full body/title/SEO fields from the production DB and cross-checked internal links against every other published post (346 total) and the marketing pages.

**1. "vps" → `/blog/what-is-a-vps`** (197 impr., pos ~27). Title/H1/first sentence all open with "A VPS — Virtual Private Server — is your own isolated slice..." — good on-page targeting, ~544 words, and reads as a solid beginner explainer. The real story here is expectation-setting: "vps" is a single high-competition dictionary term dominated by DigitalOcean, Vultr, Linode, Hostinger, Contabo, etc. Only 2 other posts link into it (`kvm-vs-openvz-virtualization-explained`, `vps-vs-cloud-hosting-whats-the-difference`), both with good exact-match anchor text ("what is a VPS"), but it has **zero placement in nav, footer, or homepage** — it's an orphan relative to the site's real link equity, and the page itself has **zero outbound internal links** despite being the natural hub for the whole VPS content cluster. Action: add 5–8 outbound links from this post into the VPS glossary cluster (choosing a VPS plan, securing a VPS, VPS vs shared/dedicated/cloud) to turn it into a genuine pillar page, and add it to the footer's "Resources" column — that's a bigger lever than rewriting copy for a term this competitive.

**2 & 4. "palworld vps" (55 impr., pos ~25) / "palworld vps hosting" (18 impr., pos ~27) → `/blog/best-vps-specs-for-a-palworld-server`**. This is a genuine intent mismatch, confirmed in code: a dedicated commercial landing page already exists at `app/(marketing)/palworld-server-hosting/page.tsx` and even links to this exact blog post as a "guide." But that landing page's title, H1, hero copy, and FAQ **never use the word "VPS" anywhere** — it's framed entirely as "Palworld server hosting." So Google has nothing better to match the VPS-flavored queries to than the informational blog post. Action: add "VPS" into the landing page's `<title>` (currently "Palworld Server Hosting — Up to 32 Players, Instant Setup"), H1/hero sub, and at least one FAQ answer (e.g., "Is Palworld hosting a VPS?") — don't build a second page, that risks cannibalizing the existing one; just recapture the terminology on the transactional page that already exists and already gets internal links.

**3. "vps for business" (22 impr., pos ~24) → `/blog/best-vps-for-a-small-business-website`**. Title says "Best VPS for a Small Business Website" — close but not exact; the query is the more generic "vps for business," and the post's own H2s/FAQ consistently say "business site" / "small business website," never the bare phrase "VPS for business." Only 2 inbound internal links (`managed-vs-unmanaged-vps`, `why-a-vps-beats-shared-hosting`), both fine anchor text. At 878 words it's reasonably deep already. Action: add one FAQ entry verbatim matching the query — "Do I need a VPS for a business?" / "Is VPS good for business?" — in the existing FAQ block (which already has 4 Qs), since FAQ schema is a cheap way to pick up an exact-phrase variant without restructuring the whole post.

**5. "ram needed for game server" (29 impr., pos ~30) → `/blog/how-much-ram-and-cpu-does-a-game-server-need`**. This one is *not* narrowly focused on one game — it genuinely covers Minecraft, Terraria/Factorio, Valheim, Project Zomboid, CS2, 7 Days to Die, Rust, V Rising/Satisfactory/Enshrouded, Palworld, and ARK, with real numbers for each, and it's the single best-internally-linked post of the five (9 other posts link into it with consistent "how much RAM and CPU a game server needs" anchor text). So thin content and narrow game focus are both ruled out. The likely blocker is simply the title/opening line phrasing — it says "How Much RAM and CPU Does a Game Server Need?" not "RAM needed for a game server," and position ~30 for a 90-day-old signal on a well-built page is plausibly just a young-page/authority timing issue rather than a content defect. Action: add a one-line variant of the exact phrase into the opening paragraph (e.g., "...here's exactly how much RAM is needed for a game server, game by game") — a low-cost tweak — but don't expect a big move; this page already looks correctly built and the fix here is a genuinely marginal add-on rather than a page rebuild.

## Part 2: New page opportunities

Read `lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts` (drives `app/(marketing)/[slug]/page.tsx`) and `lib/games.ts`.

- **Game landing pages: no gap.** All 19 entries in `GAME_FAMILIES` (`lib/games.ts:3`) have a dedicated landing page under `app/(marketing)/` — nothing to add here. (`fivem-server-hosting` exists too, outside the family list, already covered.)
- **City matrix: 18 cities × 6 services = 108 pages, + 3 regions × 6 services = 18 pages = 126 total.** Cities covered: Singapore, London, Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Paris, New York, Toronto, Los Angeles, Sydney, Tokyo, Mumbai, Dallas, Miami, Chicago, Hong Kong, Seoul, Dubai, Sao Paulo. The concrete gap: Singapore's own `LOCATIONS` entry lists Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur, Manila, and Bangkok as its explicitly-named "nearby" audience markets (`lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts:87`) — i.e., the site's own data already identifies these as the natural audience for its one real datacenter — yet none of the four has its own city page, while lower-relevance/no-datacenter markets like Sao Paulo and Dubai do. Adding Jakarta and Manila (largest SEA gaming/hosting search markets) as city+service combos is the most defensible net-new addition, since it's grounded in the site's own stated market logic, not a fabricated keyword guess.
- I checked the `SeoOpportunity` table directly (the DB-backed GSC cache behind `/admin/seo`) — it currently holds **only the 5 rows given in this task**, nothing more. So beyond those 5, there's no cached real query data to mine yet; the city-gap suggestion above is a content-architecture inference, not a GSC-backed one, and should be labeled as such to the owner.
- The one topic-level gap implied by the given data (not a new page, a positioning fix) is the Palworld VPS terminology gap covered in Part 1 — worth flagging again here since it's the clearest "demand exists, no matching page/positioning" case in this batch.

## Part 3: Sitemap

`/opt/nxeon/app/sitemap.ts` is a **hybrid — not fully dynamic**. It has a large hardcoded `staticRoutes` array (~95 explicit paths) plus genuinely dynamic sections: `LANDING_SLUGS`/`REGION_LANDING_SLUGS` are imported live from `lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts` (so the full 126-page city/region matrix, including anything added Aug 29–30, is automatically included with no manual edit needed), blog posts come from a live `db.blogPost.findMany({ published: true })` query (also fully automatic), and public free-Minecraft server pages are similarly queried live.

**Direct answer: yes, the sitemap needs a manual update** — not for the dynamic parts (those are fine and already current), but because 10 real, indexable, canonical-tagged marketing pages exist as routes under `app/(marketing)/` and are simply missing from the hardcoded `staticRoutes` list:

I confirmed each has full `metadata`/`alternates.canonical` (no noindex) — they're meant to be indexed. Notably, the sitemap already lists all 10 paired `/migrate-from-X` pages but only 2 of the 10 paired `/vps-vs-X` comparison pages (`digitalocean`, `hostinger`) — the other 8 comparison pages were evidently added after the sitemap's hardcoded list was last touched and never backfilled. (`/docs`'s public retirement per your memory note doesn't apply here — this `/docs` is the live API-reference page at `app/(marketing)/docs/page.tsx`, separate from the old public docs hub, and it's fully indexable.) `/v2` was correctly and deliberately left out per the code's own comment (noindex homepage preview).
